text.title: Build-Generator Discipline — Run Contract
text.summary: What a compliant generator run must guarantee and must print, and the separation of duties between the three modes — build, full check, deterministic check. Deliberately not a JSON schema: the artefact is a tree of files, and the contract is about the process that produced it.

section.title: Three modes, three jobs

list.item: `build` — renders everything into memory, writes atomically, repairs drift in hand-maintained files, regenerates derived artefacts, then verifies. Writes; asserts only after writing, and only about things it did not itself repair.
`--check` — renders everything and compares with disk. Writes nothing. This is the pre-push gate. It is meaningful only where the external toolchain matches the one that built the tree.
`--check-<deterministic-subset>` — the half of the check that needs no external converter: stamps, derived lists, generated manifests. This is the CI gate, because it is reproducible on any machine.

section.p: The three are separate entry points, not flags that fall through to one another. The reason is r6: a build repairs drift, so a check that runs after its own repair proves nothing, and a check folded into the build is that check.

section.title: Guarantees a build run must satisfy

list.item: g1 — either every output file is written, or none is. A failure at any point leaves the tree exactly as it was.
g2 — every source under the source directory is either mapped to an output or named in the explicit unpublished list. A third state does not exist.
g3 — no output file was produced from a converter run that emitted anything on stderr.
g4 — no output body falls below the short-body floor.
g5 — every derived artefact (precache list, index, manifest, count) was computed in this run, not read from a previous one and not transcribed.
g6 — every shared block that the generator injects into hand-maintained files is present in all of them after the run, asserted explicitly.
g7 — the run is idempotent: running it twice changes nothing, which is what makes `--check` meaningful at all.

section.title: What the run must print
section.p: Enough for the operator to notice a repair. A silent successful build hides exactly the events worth seeing.

list.item: The number of outputs written.
Every hand-maintained file whose shared block was REPAIRED, by name — that file had drifted, and a deploy without a rebuild would have shipped it broken.
Every derived artefact regenerated, with its size or item count.
Every degradation the build chose to tolerate (a muted dead link, a skipped optional source), by name.
The result of the post-write verification, not merely its absence of failure.

example.code:
$ build --check --check: 21 pages, sw.js and 6 entry points are all current
$ build 21 pages PWA head REPAIRED in trainer.html — it had drifted; a deploy without a rebuild would have shipped it broken sw.js (48 files, 3.1 MB) 2 dead link(s) muted: draft-a, draft-b verified: 6 entry points carry the head
example.note: The repair line is the whole point of printing anything: it is a defect that had already happened and would otherwise have been fixed invisibly.
Meaningless. The build repaired the drift the check then failed to find. This is r6 stated as a shell line: check first, or check in a separate run on unmodified state.

list.item: Can a mid-run failure leave the tree half-written? If yes, g1 is not met.
Is there a source that is neither built nor declared unpublished?
Does any generated number appear as a literal anywhere?
Does CI run the deterministic check rather than the full one?
Does a second consecutive build print zero repairs?
